topic.title: Line of best fit through (x̄, ȳ): drawing, equation and use
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 3 is one 1-hour calculator paper of 50 marks, sat every Summer. The line of best fit is the second half of the Spearman question in every paper read except 2025 (Summer 2019 Q6, 2021 Q4, 2022 Q2, 2023 Q1, 2024 Q2, 2026 Q2): the two means (a mark each in 2024 and 2026), the line drawn on the printed graph [2], one mark for passing through the means and one for the slope, and its equation [3], the gradient, c from the means and the equation. The data are already plotted, and the axes often start above zero.
mustMemorise: Calculate $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ and draw the line through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$
Gradient from the mean point and a second point on the line: $m = \dfrac{y_{2} - y_{1}}{x_{2} - x_{1}}$
$c = \bar{y} - m\bar{x}$, found by substituting the mean point
Estimate inside the range of the data; beyond it is extrapolation

given: Addition rule P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)

Normal Probability Table on page 3 of the booklet
mustKnow: The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x-bar, y-bar)
Gradient from two points on the line: change in y over change in x
c from substituting the mean point into y = mx + c

mustBeAbleTo: Calculate $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$, to 2 decimal places where they do not come out exactly, and plot the mean point
Draw the line of best fit through the mean point along the trend, not forced through the origin
Find the gradient from the mean point and a second point on the line, keeping its sign
Find $c$ by substituting the mean point into $y = mx + c$ and subtracting, never by reading an axis that starts above zero
Write the equation as $y = mx + c$ and use it to estimate inside the range of the data
Explain why an estimate beyond the data is extrapolation and may not be reliable

noteBlocks.lede: A scatter graph shows a trend; a line of best fit turns that trend into a rule you can use. On this paper the line always passes through one special point, the mean point. From it you find the line's equation and use it to estimate, as long as you stay inside the data.
can: Find the mean point and draw the line of best fit through it
Find the equation of the line from two points on it
Use the equation to estimate, and say when an estimate cannot be trusted

noteBlocks.text: One line through the middle of the data

noteBlocks.md:
A community garden records the hours of sunshine each week and the kilograms of tomatoes picked. More sun, more tomatoes: the crosses rise from left to right, but they do not sit exactly on a line.
A line of best fit is the straight line that follows that trend as closely as it can. Once it is drawn, its equation estimates the crop for weeks nobody recorded.

noteBlocks.caption: Eight weeks of sunshine and tomatoes. The ringed point is the mean point, and the line passes through it.

noteBlocks.md:
Each cross is one recorded week. The one furthest left sits at $x = 18$, $y = 4.8$: 18 hours of sunshine gave 4.8 kg.
The ringed point was never recorded: it is worked out from all the weeks, as the next section shows.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the garden scatter graph of sunshine and tomatoes, how many weeks are plotted?
noteBlocks.explain: Count the crosses: there is one for each week recorded, so 8. The ringed point is not a week: it is the mean point, worked out from the weeks, which comes next.

noteBlocks.md:
Work out $\bar{x}$, the mean of the $x$ values, and $\bar{y}$, the mean of the $y$ values. Together they make the mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.
Here the eight sunshine totals add up to 240, so $\bar{x} = 30$, and the eight masses add up to 51.2, so $\bar{y} = 6.4$.

noteBlocks.caption: The mean of $x$ and the mean of $y$ meet at the mean point, $(30, 6.4)$.

noteBlocks.title: Why the mean point?
noteBlocks.md: The mean point is the centre of balance of the data: a sensible line through it has the crosses above it balancing the crosses below. It is also the one point on the line you can calculate exactly, so this specification says the line must go through it, and the mark scheme checks that it does.

noteBlocks.prompt: Five values of $x$ are 12, 15, 17, 20 and 26. What is $\bar{x}$?
noteBlocks.explain: Add the values and divide by how many there are, as the garden's eight weeks were: the five add up to 90, and $\dfrac{90}{5}$ is 18. The mean point needs this for $x$ and again for $y$.

noteBlocks.text: 2. Draw the line through the mean point

noteBlocks.md: Plot the mean point, then lay your ruler through it along the trend, so that roughly as many crosses lie above the line as below it.

noteBlocks.title: Drawing the line of best fit
noteBlocks.why: A short demonstration of drawing a line of best fit by eye. On this paper, make sure yours also passes through the mean point.

noteBlocks.md: The line does not have to start at the origin, and it usually should not: forcing it through $(0, 0)$ tips it away from the data, even when it still passes through the mean point.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the garden graph with lines A and B, both drawn through the mean point, which is the line of best fit?
options: Either, because both pass through the mean point
noteBlocks.explain: Look at where the crosses sit against each line. Line A follows them, four above and four below. Line B was forced through the origin, so it runs below the crosses on the left and above them on the right, even though it also passes through the mean point.

noteBlocks.caption: Rise over run between two points on the line, the mean point and (44, 8.5).

noteBlocks.md:
Use the mean point and a second point read off your line, well away from it. Never use two plotted crosses: they are data, not points on the line.
Here the line also passes through $(44, 8.5)$, so $m = \dfrac{8.5 - 6.4}{44 - 30}$, which is $\dfrac{2.1}{14}$, so $m = 0.15$.

noteBlocks.prompt: A line of best fit passes through the mean point $(12, 20)$ and the point $(20, 30)$. What is its gradient?
noteBlocks.explain: As with the garden line, take the second point's values minus the mean point's, top and bottom in the same order: $\dfrac{30 - 20}{20 - 12}$ is $\dfrac{10}{8}$, which is 1.25. The line rises, so the gradient is positive.

noteBlocks.caption: Six used cars: the older the car, the lower its price. The line falls, so its gradient is negative.

noteBlocks.md:
When the crosses fall from left to right, so does the line. Six used cars of one model give age in years and price in thousands of pounds; the line passes through the mean point $(3.5, 14)$ and $(7, 7.7)$.
Subtract in the same order, top and bottom: $m = \dfrac{7.7 - 14}{7 - 3.5}$, which is $\dfrac{-6.3}{3.5}$, so $m = -1.8$.
Counting squares, down 6.3 and across 3.5, gives the size of the gradient but not its sign. A falling line needs the minus, and the subtraction supplies it.

noteBlocks.prompt: A line of best fit passes through the mean point $(20, 50)$ and the point $(30, 35)$. What is its gradient?
noteBlocks.explain: As with the cars, subtract in the same order top and bottom: $\dfrac{35 - 50}{30 - 20}$ is $\dfrac{-15}{10}$, which is $-1.5$. The line falls from left to right, so its gradient must be negative.

noteBlocks.text: 5. The intercept, from the mean point

noteBlocks.md:
Substitute the mean point and your gradient into $y = mx + c$, then **subtract** to find $c$:
$6.4 = 0.15 \times 30 + c$, so $c = 6.4 - 4.5$, which is 1.9, and the line is $y = 0.15x + 1.9$.
Do not read $c$ off the graph: exam graphs often start their axes above zero.

noteBlocks.title: Subtract, do not divide
noteBlocks.md: Examiners have reported $c$ found by dividing, as if $6.4 \div 4.5$ gave it, instead of subtracting, and intercepts read off graphs whose axes did not start at zero.

noteBlocks.prompt: A line of best fit has gradient 2.5 and passes through the mean point $(8, 30)$. What is $c$?
noteBlocks.explain: Substitute the mean point and the gradient, then subtract, as for the garden: $30 = 2.5 \times 8 + c$, which is $30 = 20 + c$, so $c = 30 - 20$, which is 10. Dividing 30 by 20 would give 1.5, which is not how an equation is solved.

noteBlocks.md:
To estimate, substitute into the equation. For 26 hours of sunshine, $0.15 \times 26 + 1.9 = 5.8$, so about 5.8 kg.
That is **interpolation**: 26 lies inside the recorded range, 18 to 44 hours, so the estimate can be trusted. For 60 hours the sum still gives $0.15 \times 60 + 1.9 = 10.9$, but that is **extrapolating** beyond the data, where nobody knows whether the trend carries on.

noteBlocks.prompt: Use $y = 0.15x + 1.9$ to estimate the mass of tomatoes, in kilograms, for a week with 36 hours of sunshine.
noteBlocks.explain: Put 36 in place of $x$, as for 26 hours above: $0.15 \times 36 + 1.9$ is 7.3 kg. The estimate comes from the line, not from the nearest cross.

noteBlocks.prompt: The garden's line is used to estimate the crop for a week with 60 hours of sunshine. Why is that estimate unreliable?
options: 60 hours is outside the range of the data
The line does not pass through the origin
noteBlocks.answer: 60 hours is outside the range of the data
noteBlocks.explain: On the range picture, the data run from 18 to 44 hours. Beyond that, nothing shows the trend continues, so using the line there is extrapolation, and the estimate cannot be trusted.

noteBlocks.md:
Eight pupils give their hours of revision, $x$, and test marks, $y$: the paper's chain of means, line and equation.
**Means.** $\bar{x} = \dfrac{56}{8}$, which is 7; $\bar{y} = \dfrac{416}{8}$, which is 52.
**Line.** Through $(7, 52)$ along the crosses; it also passes through $(12, 69.5)$.

**Gradient.** $m = \dfrac{69.5 - 52}{12 - 7}$, which is 3.5.
**Intercept.** $52 = 3.5 \times 7 + c$, so $c = 52 - 24.5$, which is 27.5.
**Equation.** $y = 3.5x + 27.5$.

noteBlocks.prompt: The revision line of best fit is $y = 3.5x + 27.5$. Estimate the test mark for a pupil who revised for 10 hours.
noteBlocks.explain: Substitute 10 for $x$, as the garden estimate did: $3.5 \times 10 + 27.5$ is 62.5. 10 hours lies inside the data, 2 to 11 hours, so this is interpolation.

noteBlocks.md: **Axes that start above zero.** The 2021, 2023, 2024 and 2026 graphs began at 50, 60, 30 and 20. On the garden axes from 15, the line meets the printed axis at $0.15 \times 15 + 1.9$, which is 4.15: that is not $c$.
**Points from the table.** Reports in 2019, 2022, 2023 and 2024 describe gradients worked from plotted crosses. Use the mean point and a point read off your own line.

noteBlocks.prompt: A printed scatter graph has axes starting at 30. Your line meets the vertical axis there at 34. How do you find $c$?
options: Substitute the mean point and the gradient into $y = mx + c$
Use the first two points in the table
noteBlocks.answer: Substitute the mean point and the gradient into $y = mx + c$
noteBlocks.explain: That vertical axis stands at $x = 30$, not at $x = 0$, so 34 is the value of $y$ at $x = 30$, just as 4.15 was on the garden axes from 15. The intercept comes from substituting the mean point and the gradient into $y = mx + c$.

noteBlocks.md:
Draw the line through the mean point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, never forced through the origin.
Find the gradient from two points on your line, the mean point one of them.
Give a falling line its negative gradient: subtract in the same order, top and bottom.
Find $c$ by substituting the mean point and subtracting, never by reading an axis that starts above zero.
Estimate inside the range of the data; beyond it is extrapolation.

This is usually the second half of the Spearman question: the two means for a mark each, your line through the mean point for two, then its equation for three. The first marks are for the mean point and a line through it; the last is the equation. Stuck: take the gradient from the mean point and one other point on your line, then substitute the mean point to find c.

Use the mean point and the second point on the line, subtracting in the same order top and bottom. The line falls, so a negative gradient is what you expect.

options: The mean point and another point on the line
The first and last weeks in the table
The origin and the mean point
whyMenu.explain: The equation describes the line, so both points must be on the line. Table points are data, and the line need not pass through the origin.

steps.decision: Substitute the mean point and subtract to find $c$. Multiplying by a negative gradient makes that term negative, so $c$ comes out larger than $\bar{y}$.
Put the gradient and the intercept you found into $y = mx + c$.
5 degrees C lies inside the recorded range, 2 to 12 degrees C, so this is interpolation and the estimate can be trusted.

steps.decision: Start with the mean point: the line passes through it, and it is the one point you can calculate rather than read.
Use the mean point and the second point on the line, subtracting in the same order top and bottom. The line rises, so the gradient is positive.
Substitute the mean point and subtract. $c$ comes out negative, which is fine: the line would cross $x = 0$ below the axis, far to the left of the printed graph, which starts at 10.

options: Substituting the mean point, because the printed axis stands at x = 10, not at x = 0
Reading where the line meets the printed vertical axis
Taking c as positive, because a number of ice creams cannot be negative
whyMenu.explain: Where the line meets the printed axis is the value of $y$ at $x = 10$, which is 1, not $c$. And $c$ is only a number in the equation: no day at 0 °C was recorded, so a negative value there says nothing about real sales.

steps.decision: Put the gradient and the intercept into $y = mx + c$, keeping the minus sign on the constant.
21 °C lies inside the recorded range, 14 to 24 °C, so this is interpolation and the estimate can be trusted.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $y = 5x - 49$, and about 56 ice creams on a day of 21 °C

twin.stem:
A line of best fit passes through the mean point $(8, 20)$ and the point $(12, 26)$.
Find its equation.

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on earlier work. What is the gradient of the straight line through $(2, 5)$ and $(6, 13)$?
items.skill: Gradient between two points (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: Yes: $\dfrac{13 - 5}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2$. The gradient of a line of best fit is found exactly this way.
That is the change in $x$ over the change in $y$. Gradient is the change in $y$ over the change in $x$.
That is the change in $y$ on its own. Divide it by the change in $x$, which is 4.

items.stem: Another check on earlier work. What is the mean of 4, 6, 11 and 15?
items.skill: The mean of a list (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: That is the total. Divide it by how many values there are.
That is the median, the middle of the ordered list. The mean is the total divided by the number of values.

items.stem: One more from earlier work. Solve $6.4 = 6 + c$.
items.skill: Solving a one-step equation (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: Yes: take 6 from both sides. This is exactly how the intercept is found.
That adds 6 instead of taking it away. Undo $+ 6$ by subtracting 6.
That divides 6.4 by 6, but $c$ is added to 6, not multiplied by it. Subtract instead.

items.stem: On this specification, a line of best fit must pass through which point?

options.feedback: Yes. It is the one point you can calculate exactly, and the mark scheme checks the line passes through it.
Nothing makes a line of best fit pass through the origin; examiners report marks lost for lines forced through it.
A single data point is just one cross. The line goes through the mean point, which balances all of them.

items.stem: A line of best fit passes through $(2, 30)$ and $(6, 18)$. What is its gradient?

options.feedback: Yes: $\dfrac{18 - 30}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{-12}{4} = -3$. The line falls, so the gradient is negative.
The size is right but the sign is lost: $y$ falls by 12 as $x$ rises by 4, so the gradient is $-3$.
That is upside down: change in $x$ over change in $y$. Gradient is change in $y$ over change in $x$.

items.stem: To find the gradient of your line of best fit, which two points should you use?

options.text: The mean point and another point on your line
options.feedback: Yes. The equation describes the line, so both points must be on it.

options.text: The first and last points in the table
options.feedback: Those are data points, and they are usually not on the line. Examiners report this in several years.

options.text: The two crosses closest to the line
options.feedback: Close is not on. Read the second point off the line itself.

items.stem: A line of best fit has gradient 1.5 and passes through the mean point $(12, 25)$. What is $c$?

options.feedback: That is $25 \div 18$. The 18 is added to $c$, so subtract it: $c = 25 - 18 = 7$.
That is $25 \div 12$, which ignores the gradient. Substitute into $y = mx + c$ and subtract: $c = 7$.

items.stem: On a graph whose axes start at 30, a line of best fit meets the vertical axis at $y = 38$. What does the 38 tell you?

options.text: The value of $y$ when $x = 30$, not the intercept
options.feedback: Yes. The intercept is the value of $y$ when $x = 0$, which is off this graph; find it by substituting the mean point.

options.text: The intercept $c$, because it is where the line meets the vertical axis
options.feedback: Only when the vertical axis stands at $x = 0$. Here it stands at $x = 30$, and examiners report exactly this misreading.

options.text: The intercept $c$, as long as the line passes through the mean point
options.feedback: Passing through the mean point does not move the axis. Where the axis starts is what matters, and here it starts at 30.

items.stem: A mean works out as $47.2857\ldots$. How should it be written on this paper?

options.feedback: Yes: 2 decimal places unless the question says otherwise.
Rounding to a whole number loses the mark. Give 2 decimal places: 47.29.
That cuts the value off instead of rounding it. The third decimal is 5, so round up: 47.29.

parts.stem:
The table shows the minutes seven pupils spent on homework one evening, $x$, and their minutes of screen time that evening, $y$.
Calculate $\bar{x}$.
hints: Add the seven homework times.
Divide by 7.
parts.workedSolution:
The seven homework times add up to 280.
$\bar{x} = \dfrac{280}{7}$
$= 40$

parts.stem: Calculate $\bar{y}$.
hints: Add the seven screen times and divide by 7.
Give the answer to 2 decimal places, as the paper's front page asks.
parts.workedSolution:
The seven screen times add up to 631.
$\bar{y} = \dfrac{631}{7}$
$= 90.14$ to 2 decimal places.

commonErrors.feedback: 90 is the mean rounded to a whole number. On this paper answers go to 2 decimal places unless the question says otherwise: $\bar{y} = 90.14$.

On the grid, plot the mean point and draw the line of best fit.
hints: Plot the mean point first.
Lay the line through the mean point and the second point given.
parts.workedSolution: Plot $(10, 8)$, then draw the straight line through it and $(20, 13)$. It runs up through the middle of the crosses, with about as many above it as below.

commonErrors.feedback: A line of best fit does not have to start at the origin. Forced through $(0, 0)$ it tilts away from the crosses; draw it through the mean point along the trend instead.

The graph shows the charge left on a phone, $y$ per cent, after $x$ hours of use, with a line of best fit drawn through the mean point $(4, 64)$ and the point $(7.5, 36)$.
Calculate the gradient of the line of best fit.
hints: Use the two points on the line, not two crosses.
The line slopes down, so expect a negative gradient.

commonErrors.feedback: The line slopes down, so its gradient is negative: $\dfrac{-28}{3.5} = -8$. Counting rise over run in squares loses that sign; subtracting in the same order keeps it.
That gradient comes from the first and last crosses, $(1, 89)$ and $(7, 39)$, which are data, not points on the line. Use the two points on the line: $-8$.

parts.stem:
The line of best fit for the phone has gradient $-8$ and passes through the mean point $(4, 64)$.
Find the value of $c$ in $y = mx + c$.
hints: Put the mean point and the gradient into $y = mx + c$.
$-8 \times 4$ is negative.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 64 divided by $-8 \times 4$. Substituting gives $64 = -32 + c$, and $c$ is found by adding 32 to both sides: $c = 96$.
The minus sign of the gradient was lost: $-8 \times 4 = -32$, so $64 = -32 + c$ and $c = 96$.

parts.stem:
For the eight taxi journeys the mean point is $(10, 8)$, and the line of best fit also passes through $(20, 13)$.

hints: Gradient first, from the two points given.
Then put the mean point into $y = mx + c$ to find $c$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient is upside down: run over rise gives 2. Rise over run is $\dfrac{5}{10} = 0.5$, and then $c = 3$.
The gradient is right, but $c$ was found by dividing 8 by 5. From $8 = 5 + c$, subtract: $c = 3$.

The graph shows eight pupils' mock marks, $x$, and final marks, $y$, with the line of best fit drawn through the mean point $(50, 54)$ and the point $(70, 70)$. Its gradient is $0.8$.
Find the value of $c$ in $y = mx + c$.
hints: Where does the vertical axis on this graph stand: at $x = 0$?
Substitute the mean point instead of reading the graph.
parts.workedSolution:
The printed vertical axis stands at $x = 30$, so it cannot show $c$.
$54 = 0.8 \times 50 + c$
$54 = 40 + c$
$c = 14$

commonErrors.feedback: 38 is where the line meets the printed vertical axis, but that axis stands at $x = 30$, not $x = 0$. Substitute the mean point instead: $c = 14$.
That is 54 divided by $0.8 \times 50$. Substitute and subtract: $c = 54 - 40 = 14$.

parts.stem:
The table and the scatter graph show the maximum temperature, $x$ degrees C, and the number of swimmers, $y$, at an outdoor pool on ten days.
Calculate $\bar{x}$.
hints: Add the ten temperatures and divide by 10.

parts.stem: Calculate $\bar{y}$.
hints: Add the ten numbers of swimmers and divide by 10.

parts.stem:
The line of best fit through the mean point also passes through $(30, 290)$.
On the grid, plot the mean point and draw the line of best fit.

scheme.for: the mean point $(22, 170)$ plotted, for the line to pass through
the slope: the line also passes through $(30, 290)$

hints: Plot the mean point from part (a).
Then lay the line through it and the second point.
parts.workedSolution: Plot $(22, 170)$ and draw the straight line through it and $(30, 290)$, running up through the middle of the crosses.

commonErrors.feedback: The line was forced through the origin. A line of best fit follows the data through the mean point; nothing makes it pass through $(0, 0)$, and here it does not.

parts.stem: Find the equation of this line. Write it as $y = mx + c$.
hints: Use the mean point and the other point on the line.
Then substitute the mean point to find $c$.

commonErrors.feedback: That gradient comes from the first and last crosses, $(16, 86)$ and $(28, 254)$. They are data, not points on the line; use the mean point and $(30, 290)$: $m = 15$, $c = -160$.

parts.stem: Use your equation to estimate the number of swimmers on a day when the maximum temperature is 27 degrees C.
hints: Substitute the temperature into your equation.

parts.stem: Explain why the equation should not be used to estimate the number of swimmers on a day when the maximum temperature is 5 degrees C.

accepted: 5 degrees C is outside the range of the data, which runs from 16 to 28 degrees C, so this would be extrapolation; the equation even gives a negative number of swimmers.

scheme.for: 5 degrees C is outside the range of the data (extrapolation); accept that the equation gives $-85$ swimmers

hints: Compare 5 degrees C with the temperatures recorded.
What does the equation give at 5 degrees C?
parts.workedSolution: 5 degrees C is outside the range of the data, which runs from 16 to 28 degrees C, so using the line there is extrapolation. It even gives $15 \times 5 - 160 = -85$, a negative number of swimmers.

parts.stem:
The table shows the weekly hours of part-time work, $x$, and the weekly hours of revision, $y$, of seven pupils.
Calculate $\bar{x}$.
hints: Add the seven hours of work.
Divide by 7.
parts.workedSolution:
The seven hours of work add up to 70.
$\bar{x} = \dfrac{70}{7}$
$= 10$

parts.stem: Calculate $\bar{y}$.
hints: Add the seven hours of revision and divide by 7.
parts.workedSolution:
The seven hours of revision add up to 77.
$\bar{y} = \dfrac{77}{7}$
$= 11$

parts.stem:
The line of best fit passes through the mean point and through $(18, 5.4)$. On the printed graph the horizontal axis starts at 2.
Find the equation of the line. Write it as $y = mx + c$.
hints: The line falls, so expect a negative gradient: subtract in the same order, top and bottom.
The axis starts at 2, so find $c$ by substituting the mean point.

commonErrors.feedback: The revision hours fall as the work hours rise, so the gradient is negative: $m = -0.7$. Subtracting in the same order, top and bottom, gives the minus, and then $c = 18$.
The gradient is right, but 16.6 is where the line meets the printed vertical axis, which stands at $x = 2$, not at $x = 0$. Substitute the mean point instead: $c = 18$.

parts.stem: Use your equation to estimate the weekly hours of revision of a pupil who works 9.5 hours a week.
hints: Substitute the hours of work into your equation.

commonErrors.feedback: 11 hours is the revision of the pupil who works 10 hours, the nearest in the table. The estimate comes from the line: $-0.7 \times 9.5 + 18$, which is 11.35.

parts.stem: A teacher uses the same line for a pupil who works 25 hours a week and a pupil who works 9.5 hours a week. Which estimate can be trusted?

options.text: The estimate for 9.5 hours, which lies inside the data
options.feedback: Yes: 9.5 hours is between 4 and 16, so this is interpolation. 25 hours is beyond the data.

options.text: The estimate for 25 hours, because the line carries on
options.feedback: The data stop at 16 hours. Beyond that nothing shows the trend continues, so 25 hours is extrapolation and cannot be trusted.

options.text: Neither, because the line does not pass through the origin
options.feedback: A line of best fit does not have to pass through the origin. What matters is whether the value lies inside the range of the data.

scheme.for: the 9.5 hours estimate, inside the data

hints: The data run from 4 to 16 hours of work.
parts.workedSolution: 9.5 hours lies inside the data, 4 to 16 hours, so that estimate is interpolation. 25 hours lies beyond it: extrapolation.

context.setting: A line of best fit on axes that start at 40 and 20

parts.stem:
A line of best fit passes through the mean point $(45, 30)$ and the point $(65, 62)$.
Find the gradient of the line.
hints: Change in $y$ on top, change in $x$ underneath.
Subtract in the same order, top and bottom.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.625 is the run over the rise, the fraction upside down. The gradient is the change in $y$ over the change in $x$: $\dfrac{32}{20}$, which is 1.6.

parts.stem:
The printed graph's axes start at 40 and 20.
Find the equation of the line. Write it as $y = mx + c$.
hints: The vertical axis stands at $x = 40$, so it cannot show $c$.
Substitute the mean point and subtract.

commonErrors.feedback: That uses the gradient upside down, the run over the rise. The gradient is 1.6; substituting the mean point then gives $c = -42$.
The gradient is right, but 22 is where the line meets the printed vertical axis, at $x = 40$. The intercept is at $x = 0$: substitute the mean point to get $c = -42$.

parts.stem: Use your equation to estimate $y$ when $x = 55$.
hints: Substitute the value of $x$ into your equation.

findTheMistake.stem: Conor's line of best fit passes through the mean point $(12, 20)$ and the point $(20, 30)$, and he was asked for its equation. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 divides 20 by 15. Line 2 says 20 = 15 + c, so $c$ is what is added to 15 to make 20: $c = 20 - 15 = 5$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The gradient and the substitution are right, so both method marks stand; only the final working mark is lost. A quick check catches the slip: at $x = 12$ the line should give the mean, 20, but $1.25 \times 12 + 1.33 = 16.33$. The equation is $y = 1.25x + 5$.

findTheMistake.stem: Rhian's line of best fit on a scatter graph that falls from left to right passes through the mean point $(30, 42)$ and the point $(50, 30)$. She was asked for its equation. Her working:
studentWorking: From (30, 42) to (50, 30) the line goes across 20 and down 12
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 drops the sign. The line goes down 12, so the change in $y$ is −12, and $m$ is negative. Subtracting in the same order, top and bottom, supplies the minus: $\dfrac{30 - 42}{50 - 30}$, which is −0.6.
findTheMistake.feedback: Her substitution is the right method and keeps its mark with her gradient; the gradient's mark and the final equation are lost. A check would have caught it: the crosses fall from left to right, so a positive gradient cannot be right.

prompts.prompt: Which point must a line of best fit pass through on this specification?
prompts.answer: The mean point: the mean of the x values with the mean of the y values.

prompts.prompt: Which two points do you use to find the gradient of your line of best fit?
prompts.answer: The mean point and a second point read off the line itself, never two plotted points from the table.

prompts.prompt: Why should you not read c off an exam graph?
prompts.answer: The axes often start above zero, so the line meets the printed axis somewhere other than x = 0.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between interpolation and extrapolation?
prompts.answer: Interpolation estimates inside the range of the data and can be trusted; extrapolation goes beyond the data, where the trend may not continue.

prompts.prompt: A line of best fit slopes down. What sign must its gradient have, and how do you make sure you get it?
prompts.answer: Negative. Subtract in the same order on the top and on the bottom of the gradient fraction.

prompts.prompt: Does a line of best fit have to pass through the origin?
prompts.answer: No. It passes through the mean point along the trend; forcing it through the origin tips it away from the data.

prompts.prompt: Once you have the gradient, how do you find $c$?
prompts.answer: Substitute the mean point and the gradient into y = mx + c, then subtract to find c.

findings.asked: Ranks, Spearman's coefficient, interpretation, means, line of best fit and its equation.
findings.wentWrong: Tied ranks mishandled; the 6 left out of the formula, or n squared - 1 miscalculated; 'correlation' omitted from the interpretation; means rounded wrongly; lines not through the means; equations found from table points rather than points on the line; rise over run without the negative sign.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Drew the line through the mean point, took two points on the line (one being the mean point), used the gradient formula, then found c.
findings.rule: Use points ON the line, one of them the mean point.

findings.asked: Spearman and line of best fit.
findings.wentWrong: (sum d) squared used instead of sum of d squared; 'correlation' omitted; lines not through the means; table points used for the equation.

findings.asked: Spearman and line of best fit.
findings.wentWrong: d squared errors; lines forced through the origin lost a mark; c found by dividing instead of subtracting.
findings.rule: The line goes through (mean x, mean y), not necessarily the origin.

findings.asked: Spearman and line of best fit.
findings.wentWrong: Negative d squared; formula misused; 'perfect positive correlation' claimed wrongly; gradient inverted; intercept read from the graph with a truncated axis.
findings.rule: Find c by substituting the mean point, not by reading the axis.

findings.asked: Spearman with a three-way tie; interpretation.
findings.wentWrong: Three-way tied ranks; negative d squared; forgetting the '1 -' or putting it in the numerator; any positive value called 'positive correlation' although values between -0.4 and 0.4 count as weak or no correlation for this specification.
findings.rule: Tied values share the average of their positions; between -0.4 and 0.4 is weak or no correlation.

insight.ruleToRemember: Rank with averaged ties, square each d, use the formula with n(n squared - 1); interpret with the word 'correlation' and the -0.4 to 0.4 weak band; draw the line through the mean point and find its equation from two points on the line.
